By the middle of the eighteenth century the town had grown into a small but busy port, with warehouses along the quay, a rope walk behind the church, and a market square where farmers from the surrounding valleys brought their produce on Saturday mornings. The railway reached Marlowe Bay in 1874, and the arrival of the trains changed the character of the town almost overnight. The light in winter is grey and soft, and the hills behind the town disappear into mist for days at a time. In summer the evenings are long, and the sun sets behind the western headland, throwing a path of gold across the water that can be seen from the far end of the promenade. The museum beside the quay keeps a collection of photographs that record the town as it looked before the railway came, and the archivist there is always glad to explain how the harbor walls were rebuilt after the great storm of 1912. It is a landscape that rewards slow looking, and many of those who come for a week return for a lifetime.
